name: Kimura
description: Master the Kimura shoulder lock in BJJ. Complete guide covering grip mechanics, finishing technique, defensive escapes, and applications from multiple positions.

disambiguations.name: Americana
disambiguations.reason: the Americana rotates the shoulder forward (opposite figure-four direction)

target_area: Shoulder joint, rotator cuff, and shoulder capsule
variant_uniqueness: Figure-four grip enables attacks from every position
summary: The Kimura is a figure-four shoulder lock that rotates the opponent's arm behind their back to attack the rotator cuff and shoulder capsule, usable as both a finish and a controlling grip from nearly every position in grappling.
overview: The Kimura is one of the most versatile and high-percentage shoulder locks in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, named after judoka Masahiko Kimura who famously used it to defeat Helio Gracie in 1951. This figure-four grip shoulder lock attacks the opponent's arm by rotating it behind their back, creating severe pressure on the shoulder joint, rotator cuff muscles, and shoulder capsule. What makes the Kimura exceptional is its applicability from virtually every position in grappling - top, bottom, standing, or transitional - making it a fundamental technique that spans all belt levels. The Kimura serves dual purposes: as a direct finishing submission and as a powerful control position that opens numerous sweeps, transitions, and secondary attacks. The grip itself creates such dominant control that even without completing the submission, practitioners can use it to manipulate opponents, take the back, or advance position. The mechanical advantage generated by the figure-four grip allows smaller practitioners to control and submit larger opponents through proper technique rather than strength alone.

injury_risks.injury: Rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis)

injury_risks.recovery_time: 6-12 weeks for strain, 3-6 months for rupture

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training, allowing partner time to recognize danger and tap
tap_signals: Verbal tap (saying 'tap' or making any verbal distress sound)
Physical hand tap (multiple taps with free hand)
Physical foot tap (multiple taps with either foot)
Any distress signal including screaming or unusual sounds
release_protocol: Immediately stop all rotational pressure the instant tap is felt or heard
Return the arm toward neutral position (externally rotate back to starting position)
Allow partner to self-assess shoulder mobility before continuing
Never release suddenly or allow arm to spring back forcefully
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the submission - rotation must be smooth and controlled
Never use competition speed or surprise attacks in training
Always ensure partner has at least one hand free to tap
Do not apply while partner is in awkward body position that prevents tapping
Never combine with weight pressure that restricts breathing while finishing
Respect immediate taps without testing partner's pain tolerance

variations_and_setups.description: Opponent postures in your closed guard. Break their posture by pulling their head down and attacking the posting arm. Secure the Kimura grip and either finish by opening your guard and rotating, or use the grip to sweep them over your shoulder.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent posts their hand on the mat or reaches for grips, exposing their arm

variations_and_setups.description: Classic position for Kimura. Opponent's near arm is isolated as they frame or attempt to escape. Slide your under-arm through, secure the grip, and rotate their hand toward their back while maintaining chest pressure.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Most common and highest percentage position when opponent frames with near arm

variations_and_setups.description: When opponent frames or benches to create space from mount, attack the extended arm. Secure the grip and either finish from mount or use it to transition to S-mount for better leverage.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When mounted opponent pushes or frames, extending their arm

variations_and_setups.description: Secure the Kimura grip on opponent's underhook or crossface arm. Use the control to prevent their pass and either sweep them using the grip as leverage or transition to the back as they defend.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Essential half guard technique when opponent commits to underhook or crossface

variations_and_setups.description: Opponent is in turtle and posts an arm for base. Secure the Kimura grip and use it to roll them to their side or back, maintaining the grip throughout the rotation for a finish or back take.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When turtle opponent posts an arm wide for base, creating the opportunity

variations_and_setups.description: During standing exchanges, secure the Kimura grip on opponent's lead arm. Use it to control their posture and either throw them with the grip or take them down while maintaining control.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: In stand-up exchanges when opponent reaches or posts their arm

variations_and_setups.description: Transition to North-South and isolate the near arm. Secure the Kimura grip with modified body positioning and rotate their hand toward their own hip, using your body weight for control.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Natural transition from side control or when opponent turns into you

variations_and_setups.description: Instead of rotating their hand toward their back, rotate it toward their head and away from their body. This creates wristlock pressure combined with shoulder rotation.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When traditional Kimura angle is blocked but you maintain the grip

variations_and_setups.description: From standing or scrambling positions, secure the grip and initiate a rolling motion, using momentum to take opponent to the mat while maintaining the Kimura control throughout the roll.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: During scrambles or when opponent resists static Kimura attempts
